base_instruction: You are a helpful assistant for planning group activities and food. Help the user coordinate snack planning for a children's summer camp session. When the user asks you to evaluate specific snack items, check each item against every child's current dietary constraints. Pay close attention to changes in the group roster and any updates or corrections to dietary information throughout the conversation.

Anaphylaxis to cashews → severe tree nut allergy
Tree nut allergy → must avoid cashews and likely other tree nuts (cross-reactivity risk)

hidden_state.value: You are a parent organizing snacks for a neighborhood summer camp with several kids. You will introduce the kids and their dietary needs in a burst, then updates will come in: a new kid joins, one kid's constraint gets corrected/upgraded (lactose intolerance → milk protein allergy), and one kid leaves partway through the week but needs snacks packed. At the end you will share a specific snack list and ask if there are any issues. You must NEVER hint that you already know which snacks are problematic.

You are a calm, friendly parent coordinator. You relay information from other parents in third person (e.g., 'Tyler's mom told me...', 'Mason's mom texted me...'). You never express frustration even when details keep changing. You treat corrections and roster changes as totally normal summer camp coordination.
hidden_state.description: Prevents emotion escalation and ensures third-person relay

ground_truth.answer: Six snacks evaluated against current constraints: (1) Rice cakes with almond butter — fine for everyone (rice is gluten-free, almond butter is dairy-free, no root vegetables, low sugar relative to other snacks). (2) String cheese sticks — problematic for Mason, who has a milk protein allergy (not just lactose intolerance — his mom corrected this with his allergist, so all dairy is off limits). (3) Oatmeal raisin cookies — problematic for Tyler because oats are often cross-contaminated with gluten and cookies contain wheat flour (celiac disease). This also matters for his take-home snacks on Tuesday. (4) Trail mix with cashews and dried mango — problematic for Aiden, who had an anaphylactic reaction to cashews requiring an EpiPen. (5) Carrot and celery sticks with hummus — hummus typically contains garlic, which is a root vegetable forbidden in devout Jain practice, making this problematic for Sophia. (6) Fruit popsicles made with juice and sugar — problematic for Lily, who has type 1 diabetes and whose parents are careful about sugar; juice-and-sugar popsicles are high in sugar.
required_elements: String cheese sticks are problematic for Mason because he has a milk protein allergy (not just lactose intolerance — the constraint was upgraded by his mom after consulting his allergist)
Oatmeal raisin cookies are problematic for Tyler because of his celiac disease (cookies contain gluten), and this applies to his take-home snacks for Tuesday as well
Trail mix with cashews is problematic for Aiden because he has a severe cashew/tree nut allergy (anaphylactic reaction, EpiPen used)
Carrot and celery sticks with hummus are problematic for Sophia because hummus typically contains garlic, and as a devout Jain she cannot eat root vegetables including garlic
Fruit popsicles made with juice and sugar are problematic for Lily because she has type 1 diabetes and her parents are careful about sugar
Rice cakes with almond butter are fine for everyone currently in the group
forbidden_elements: Treating Mason's constraint as just lactose intolerance (it was upgraded to milk protein allergy — broader scope, all dairy is off limits)
Flagging oatmeal raisin cookies as problematic for Tyler only on Wed-Fri camp days (Tyler leaves Wednesday but needs take-home snacks Tuesday, so gluten still matters for his portion)

Flagging almond butter as a tree nut problem for Aiden without distinguishing that his confirmed allergy is to cashews specifically (almonds are tree nuts but the scenario only confirms cashew reaction — however, cross-reactivity concern is reasonable to mention)
Saying Tyler has no constraints for the last three days of camp without noting his take-home snack needs on Tuesday
Ignoring Aiden entirely (late-joining entity, must be checked against all snack items)
Saying hummus is fine for everyone without checking for garlic content against Sophia's Jain dietary restrictions
ground_truth.explanation: This scenario tests entity lifecycle tracking and constraint upgrade reasoning across 9 conversational turns. Key tracking challenges: (1) BURST delivery in turn 1 — five kids with four different constraints introduced at once. (2) LATE JOIN — Aiden joins in turn 3 with a severe tree nut allergy (cashew anaphylaxis). (3) CONSTRAINT UPGRADE — Mason's constraint changes from lactose intolerance to milk protein allergy, which is broader in scope (all dairy products are now off limits, not just high-lactose ones). (4) PARTIAL EXIT with scope change — Tyler leaves camp Wednesday but needs take-home snacks Tuesday, so his celiac/gluten constraint still applies to his portion. (5) INFERENTIAL CONSTRAINTS — Tyler's celiac → no gluten (agent must know celiac = gluten autoimmune disorder), Sophia's Jain family → no meat/fish/eggs/root vegetables (agent must know devout Jain dietary rules and that garlic is a root vegetable), Aiden's cashew EpiPen reaction → severe tree nut allergy. (6) HIDDEN INGREDIENT — hummus typically contains garlic, which is a root vegetable forbidden in Jain practice (multi-step: hummus → contains garlic → garlic is root vegetable → Jain restriction). The probe includes 6 items with mixed verdicts: 1 clearly fine (rice cakes with almond butter), 4 clearly problematic for different reasons (string cheese, cookies, trail mix, popsicles), and 1 requiring hidden ingredient inference (hummus contains garlic → Sophia's Jain constraint).

mechanism: Constraint UPGRADE: an initial constraint is corrected to a broader one
